name: NEAR Shoemaker
payload: NEAR Shoemaker (805 kg at launch, 487 kg dry)
significance: NEAR Shoemaker was launched to determine whether a small, tightly-budgeted spacecraft could resolve a debate about S-type asteroids through close-range, extended orbital study of a large near-Earth object, 433 Eros, rather than a brief flyby. It became the first spacecraft to orbit an asteroid and, when its instruments outlasted expectations, the first spacecraft ever to soft-land on one -- a feat achieved by a probe never designed with landing gear. Its year in orbit showed Eros to be a solid, unfractured S-type body of roughly chondritic composition, directly linking ordinary-chondrite meteorites to a real S-type parent asteroid, while its en-route flyby of 253 Mathilde delivered the first close-up images of a primitive, dark C-type asteroid. As the first mission of NASA's low-cost Discovery program, NEAR Shoemaker proved that a small, inexpensive spacecraft could rendezvous with, orbit, and ultimately touch a small solar-system body, opening the trajectory-and-budget playbook every subsequent asteroid rendezvous mission would follow.
statusNote: Single Earth gravity-assist flyby (1998-01-23, altitude 540 km) used to reshape the trajectory toward Eros. Also imaged asteroid 253 Mathilde at a distance of 1,212 km on 1997-06-27 during the already-planned coast -- a deliberately targeted science pass, but Mathilde is far too low-mass to produce a meaningful gravity assist, so not modeled as its own leg, the same treatment Rosetta's Steins/Lutetia passes get. A rendezvous-burn abort on 1998-12-20 threw the spacecraft into safe mode and past Eros at 3,827 km instead of the planned arrival, costing 29 kg of propellant and delaying orbit insertion by over a year; a recovery burn on 1999-01-03 corrected course, and NEAR finally entered orbit around Eros on 2000-02-14. The mission ended with a historic soft landing on Eros (2001-02-12), the first landing on an asteroid by a spacecraft never designed to land.

legs._comment: Real NEAR Shoemaker trajectory (JPL Horizons, target -93, checked 2026-07) sweeps ~317 degrees around the Sun during this first Earth->Earth loop, reaching ~2.1 AU (past Mars) near 1997-04 -- close enough to a full lap, combined with a long duration, that a plain 2-point Lambert solve across the whole leg misses the real intermediate path by 0.3-0.5 AU even though the endpoints and rough sweep angle look plausible. Split through two real recorded positions so each third stays safely inside the solver's reliable range.

Real NEAR Shoemaker trajectory (JPL Horizons, target -93, checked 2026-08) sweeps ~467 degrees around the Sun between the Earth flyby and Eros orbit insertion -- more than a full revolution, since NEAR spent over a year in a near-Eros-like orbit working through the 1998-12-20 rendezvous-burn abort and 1999-01-03 recovery burn (see statusNote). A single 2-point Lambert solve across the whole span can't tell that apart from a much shorter, wildly wrong sweep -- it balloons out to ~3.2 AU (past Eros's real ~1.78 AU aphelion) instead of tracking Eros's own orbit. Split through two real recorded positions, same fix as this file's own first leg above.
